entries.text: Modules. The station is built from round modules joined end to end — each one is a room in space.
Connecting node. Where the modules meet, a round node with hatches lets astronauts walk from room to room.
Solar wings. Two huge wings of dark blue panels turn sunlight into all the electricity the station needs.
Spine truss. A long framework, the truss, carries the wings and holds them out away from the rooms.
Robot arm. A long arm with joints and a gripper reaches out to catch and hold visiting spacecraft.
Docking port. A ringed port on the nose of a module is the doorway where ships click onto the station.
Cupola. A bubble of windows looks straight down — astronauts watch Earth and guide the robot arm from here.
Portholes. Every module has its own round portholes, so there is always a window to the stars.
Cabin inside. Inside, lockers and racks line the curved wall: sleeping bag, table, treadmill and the plant box.
Radiators. Pale flat panels throw away the heat the station makes, so nothing inside gets too hot.
Module skin. Each module is a metal can, made from curved panels riveted in rings.
Stiffening rings. Ribs run around the barrel like the hoops on a wooden bucket.
Bright window. Thick glass, set deep in a metal frame, keeps the air in and shows the stars.
Handholds. Little yellow grips are bolted all over the outside for spacewalking hands.
Thruster pack. Small thrusters push the station a little, so it keeps the right way round.
Hatches. Round doors open between the node and every module.
Node collar. A reinforced collar joins the rounded node to a cabin. Bolts and seals have different jobs: holding the joint and containing the air.
Interior light. Sunlight through the portholes is not enough here, so lamps stay on inside.
Solar panel. Each wing is a grid of dark blue panels, hinged into a long row.
Cell grid. Fine gold lines run across each panel to gather the electricity.
Mast. A long white mast carries the whole wing and lets it turn towards the Sun.
Hinges. The wings left Earth folded up, then unfolded in space like a fan.
Truss beam. The truss is a lattice of thin struts, not a solid tube — light but very stiff.
Power cable. Thick cables run along the truss, carrying the current back to the modules.
Coupling joint. Each piece joins the next with a bolted joint, so the truss could be built in orbit.
Shoulder joint. One powered joint on the station wall carries the whole arm and swings it around.
Arm boom. The long white tube is the arm's upper segment, made stiff enough to reach far.
Elbow joint. A middle joint folds the arm, so it can bend like your own elbow.
Wrist. A second thin segment ends in a wrist that can twist and point.
Gripper. Two metal fingers close like a hand to take hold of a cargo ship.
Docking ring. A chased metal ring with latches is the doorway a spacecraft locks onto.
Tunnel. A short tunnel through the ring lets people crawl from the ship into the station.
Approach light. A little light beside the port shows the visiting pilot how they are lined up.
Concentric target. Concentric rings mark the centre of this illustrated docking port.
Window petals. Seven windows, one on top and six around, join like the petals of a flower.
Shield cover. Metal covers can close over the glass to keep out tiny flying rocks.
Control rail. A row of controls right under the windows drives the robot arm outside.
Window frame. A heavy metal ring takes all the pushing of the air inside.
Inner pane. This teaching model shows two separate panes. Real spacecraft use window stacks designed for pressure loads and environmental protection.
Sun shade. Soft shades are tucked beside each window, because sunrise comes 16 times a day.
Equipment racks. Square racks fill the curved wall — like bookshelves, but screwed to the wall.
Sleeping bag. There is no bed to lie on, so crew zip into a bag strapped to the wall.
Galley table. Food pouches are taped down to the table so they stay put.
Treadmill. Crew run on a treadmill with a harness holding them down.
Plant box. Green lettuce grows under purple lamps — the station's little garden.
Radiator panel. Pale panels are full of pipes, and hot fluid runs through them.
Coolant loop. The fluid loop carries heat from the racks out to the panels and back.
Crystal chamber. A sealed transparent chamber holds faceted crystals. The clear walls let the crew observe growth while keeping the samples contained.
Sample vials. Three capped vials sit in retaining rings above the instrument panel. Restraints keep samples from floating away.
Cabin services. Clipped service lines follow the cabin wall. Removable floor panels give access for inspection and maintenance.
